modules.title: Module 1: AI Basics and Safe First Steps
modules.description: AI abilities, limits, risks, and safe first uses.

screens.title: Module 1: AI Basics and Safe First Steps
screens.lead: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is already part of daily life. In this module, you will learn what AI does, how common types are different, and how to use AI with care.
outcomes: Explain AI and generative AI in plain language.
Tell the difference between rules, prediction, and generation.
Spot useful tasks, common limits, and major risks.
Choose a small, safe AI task with a human review step.

screens.title: You may already use AI every day
screens.lead: AI can help with many tasks. The best uses match one clear need with one suitable tool.

sides.title: At work
items: Draft a message from approved notes
Forecast demand or flag unusual activity

screens.title: Ask five questions before you choose a tool
screens.lead: The tool should fit the work. These questions help you judge whether an AI use is sensible and safe.

cards.title: What is the task?
cards.body: Name the exact job. For example: turn meeting notes into a first draft.

cards.title: What information?
cards.body: Know what the system will receive. Do not share private data without approval.

cards.title: How correct?
cards.body: Decide how accurate and complete the answer must be.

cards.title: What if it is wrong?
cards.body: Think about the harm, cost, delay, or confusion an error could cause.

cards.title: Who is responsible?
cards.body: Choose a person who will check the result and own the final decision.

screens.title: AI has different ways to help
screens.lead: One product may use several abilities at once. Naming the ability helps you understand the result and its risks.

cards.title: Rules
cards.body: Follow steps written by people.

cards.title: Prediction
cards.body: Estimate what is likely from patterns.

cards.title: Generation
cards.body: Create a new draft or other content.

cards.title: Retrieval
cards.body: Find useful information from a source.

cards.title: Agentic action
cards.body: Use tools to carry out allowed steps.

screens.title: Rules: follow instructions written in advance
screens.lead: A rule-based system follows clear instructions written by people. It does not decide the rules for itself.
bullets: Example: send an expense claim for review when it is above a set amount.
Rules work well when the conditions and next steps are clear.
The same input should lead to the same result each time.
Rules can fail when an unusual case was not planned for.
screens.callout: People write and approve the rules. They also decide how exceptions should be handled.

screens.title: Prediction: estimate what may happen
screens.lead: A prediction system uses patterns in past data to estimate a category, score, or likely result.
bullets: Example: estimate which customers may need extra support.
A prediction is a probability, not a promise or known fact.
The result depends on the quality and fit of the data.
People should check errors, unfair patterns, and the effect of a wrong result.
screens.callout: Use predictions to support review. Do not treat a score as a final decision about a person.

screens.title: Generative AI: make new content
screens.lead: Generative AI makes new text, images, audio, video, or code from patterns learned during training and the context you provide.
bullets: Example: create a first draft of an email from approved notes.
The output is new, but it may be based on patterns found across many examples.
A clear prompt and useful context can improve the draft.
A fluent answer may still contain false facts, missing details, or unsuitable wording.
screens.callout: Generation is useful for a first draft. A person still checks facts, tone, permission, and fit for the task.

screens.title: Retrieval and tools: find information or do a set task
screens.lead: Retrieval means finding useful information from files, search, or a database. A connected tool can also perform a set action.
bullets: Example: find the paragraph in a staff policy that answers a leave question.
A calculator tool can work out a total more reliably than language generation alone.
The source may still be old, incomplete, or not approved for the task.
The input, source, method, units, and final result still need a check.
screens.callout: Using a source or tool can improve an answer, but it does not remove the need for human review.

screens.title: Agentic action: carry out several steps
screens.lead: An AI agent can plan or take a set of steps toward a goal. It may read files, use tools, or prepare an action.
bullets: Example: read sample files, group the information, and prepare a draft report.
The agent should have only the access it truly needs.
Important steps should create a record that people can review.
High-impact actions should stop for human approval before they happen.
screens.callout: More access creates more risk. Give an agent clear limits, stop rules, and approval points.

screens.title: Most AI tasks follow a simple flow
screens.lead: The details can be complex, but this four-part view helps you ask better questions.

cards.title: Input
cards.body: A request, file, image, number, sound, or other information enters the system.

cards.title: Process
cards.body: The system uses written rules, learned patterns, sources, or tools.

cards.title: Output
cards.body: It returns a draft, score, answer, match, warning, or action.

cards.title: Human check
cards.body: A person reviews the result based on the task and the risk.

screens.title: A model is not the same as a complete product
screens.lead: A product may add tools and controls around a model. Always ask which part is doing the work.

sides.title: Base model
items: Works with patterns learned in training
May generate language or other content
Does not automatically know your files or rules

sides.title: Complete product
items: May add web search or approved files
May add calculators, code, or databases
May store memory or connect to other systems
May use settings, permissions, and safety controls

screens.title: Which capability is doing the main job?
screens.lead: A system reads customer messages and places each one into Billing, Technical Help, or General Question.
bullets: A. Rules
B. Prediction or classification
C. Generation
D. Agentic action
screens.callout: Best answer: B. The system is predicting the category that best matches each message. A complete workflow may also use rules to route it afterward.

screens.title: Intelligence includes several skills
screens.lead: There is no one perfect meaning for intelligence. These five skills give us a good place to start.

cards.title: Learning
cards.body: Use new information later, even in a different situation.

cards.title: Problem solving
cards.body: Find a path to a goal when the answer is not obvious.

cards.title: Reasoning
cards.body: Use facts and evidence to reach a sound conclusion.

cards.title: Perception
cards.body: Turn sights, sounds, or other signals into useful meaning.

cards.title: Language
cards.body: Understand and produce words that fit the situation.

screens.title: Human intelligence and machine ability are not the same
screens.lead: An AI system may beat people on one narrow test. That does not mean it has human understanding.

sides.title: People bring
items: Values and a sense of what matters
The ability to question the goal

sides.title: AI systems bring
items: Fast work on a defined task
The ability to follow set rules
The same hidden errors at large scale

screens.title: What AI is - and what it is not
screens.lead: AI means computer systems that do tasks linked to human intelligence, such as language, images, prediction, or recommendations.

screens.title: The first big ideas took shape over many years
screens.lead: AI did not appear all at once. It grew from work in math, psychology, computing, and engineering.

events.body: McCulloch and Pitts describe a simple math model of brain cells.
Alan Turing suggests testing a machine through written conversation.
The Dartmouth project helps name AI as a field of study.
Early learning machines and checkers programs draw attention.
Rule-based programs and expert systems enter research and business.

screens.title: New tools and more data helped AI grow
screens.lead: New methods mattered. Larger sets of data, faster computer chips, and strong teams mattered too.

events.body: Early limits lead to less funding and the first AI winter.
Expert systems rise, then another winter follows unmet promises.
IBM Deep Blue defeats world chess champion Garry Kasparov.
AlexNet shows a major jump in image recognition.
Transformers improve how systems work with long text sequences.
Generative AI reaches millions of everyday users.

screens.title: Many people and teams helped build AI
screens.lead: These names are useful guideposts. Each new step also relied on older ideas, teams, data, computer parts, money, and testing.

cards.title: Alan Turing
cards.body: Linked computing with questions about intelligent behavior.

cards.title: John McCarthy
cards.body: Helped name AI and organize the 1956 Dartmouth project.

cards.title: Newell and Simon
cards.body: Built early programs that worked through reasoning problems.

cards.title: Arthur Samuel
cards.body: Built a checkers program and helped spread the term machine learning.

cards.title: Hinton, LeCun, Bengio
cards.body: Advanced neural-network methods used in deep learning.

cards.title: Li and ImageNet teams
cards.body: Built a large image dataset that supported computer vision progress.

cards.title: Transformer team
cards.body: Introduced an approach that became key to modern language models.

screens.title: The Turing Test measures imitation
screens.lead: A judge sends written messages to unseen partners and tries to tell which partner is a machine.

sides.title: It may show
items: The machine can hold a conversation
It can be hard to identify in that test

sides.title: It does not prove
items: It is safe for a real decision

screens.title: What is an AI winter?
screens.lead: An AI winter is a time when excitement, money, and support for AI fall sharply.
bullets: Big promises create high hopes.
Early demos work in small or controlled settings.
Real use reveals weak data, high cost, limited computers, or fragile rules.
Results do not match the promises, so projects and funding are cut.
Work may continue quietly until new ideas or tools bring fresh progress.
screens.callout: The word winter is a picture: the field becomes colder, but research does not stop completely.

screens.title: A good demo is not the same as a reliable system
screens.lead: History teaches us to match our confidence to real evidence.

cards.title: Ask what was tested
cards.body: Was it tried with real people, real data, and normal working conditions?

cards.title: Count the full cost
cards.body: Include setup, review, training, changes, and ongoing checks.

cards.title: Find the limits
cards.body: Learn when the system is likely to fail or need help.

cards.title: State uncertainty
cards.body: Be clear about what is known, unknown, and still being tested.

cards.title: Build lasting skills
cards.body: Learn how to test tools instead of chasing every new product.

screens.title: What evidence would you ask for?
screens.lead: A vendor shows an AI tool that writes a perfect customer reply in ten seconds. The vendor says it can replace all message review.
bullets: How often is the tool correct with real customer messages?
What happens with private, angry, unclear, or unusual messages?
Can a person stop or correct a message before it is sent?
What are the full setup, review, and error costs?
screens.callout: Strong answer: ask for results from the full workflow. One polished demo does not show how the tool handles everyday exceptions.

screens.title: How a language model works with text
screens.lead: These four words explain much of what happens during a chat with generative AI.

cards.title: Large language model (LLM)
cards.body: A model trained on a very large amount of text. It predicts useful next pieces of language.

cards.title: Token
cards.body: A small piece of text. It may be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation.

cards.title: Context window
cards.body: The amount of text and other information the model can work with at one time.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.body: Your request plus the details, examples, and source material you give the system.

screens.title: How AI uses sources and other media
screens.lead: A complete AI tool can do more than write text.

cards.title: Grounding
cards.body: Tie an answer to supplied or trusted sources so it has evidence to use.

cards.title: Retrieval
cards.body: Find useful material from files, search, or a database.

cards.title: Multimodal
cards.body: Work with more than text, such as images, audio, charts, or documents.

cards.title: Agent
cards.body: Plan or carry out allowed steps with tools, limits, and human checks.

screens.title: Chat, automation, and agents are not the same
screens.lead: The more a system can do on its own, the more carefully its access and checks must be designed.

cards.title: Chat assistant
cards.body: Replies to a person's messages. The person chooses each next action.

cards.title: Fixed automation
cards.body: Runs steps chosen in advance when a known event happens.

cards.title: Tool-enabled workflow
cards.body: Uses tools in a planned order, with checks between important stages.

cards.title: Agent
cards.body: Chooses or changes steps toward a limited goal. It needs tight access, records, stop rules, and approval.

screens.title: Company, app, model, and plan are different
screens.lead: You may hear names such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or Grok. Tools can change. Check the latest facts before use.

cards.title: Provider
cards.body: The company or group that offers the service.

cards.title: Product
cards.body: The app or service a person uses.

cards.title: Model
cards.body: The trained system that performs part of the work inside a product.

cards.title: Plan and settings
cards.body: The access, privacy, tools, storage, and controls available to the user or organization.

screens.title: Generative AI is useful for drafts, not guarantees
screens.lead: It creates new content from learned patterns and the context you provide.

sides.title: Never assume
items: You have permission to use it
It is fair or ready to publish

screens.title: Language generation is not the same as calculation
screens.lead: A language model is built to predict language. It may make simple math errors or use the wrong formula.
bullets: A complete product may send a math problem to a calculator, spreadsheet, or code tool.
That tool can make the calculation more dependable.
A correct calculation can still start with the wrong number, unit, date, or formula.
Check the inputs, the method, and the final answer before using it.
screens.callout: Example: 12 x 25 may be easy. A pricing model with tax, discounts, and mixed units still needs a careful human check.

screens.title: Know what can go wrong
screens.lead: Risk depends on the task, the information, the people affected, and how hard an error is to fix.

cards.title: Hallucination
cards.body: The system gives a confident answer that is false or unsupported.

cards.title: Bias
cards.body: Patterns in data or design lead to unfair results.

cards.title: Privacy
cards.body: Private information is shared, stored, or used in an unsafe way.

cards.title: Rights
cards.body: The source or output may not be allowed for your use.

cards.title: Over-reliance
cards.body: People accept the answer without enough checking.

cards.title: Accountability
cards.body: No one is clearly responsible for the choice or harm.

screens.title: AI often changes tasks before it changes whole jobs
screens.lead: The effect is different across jobs, workplaces, industries, laws, and levels of AI use.

screens.title: Spot the risk and add a safeguard
screens.lead: A team wants AI to send automatic replies to unhappy customers. The tool will use past messages and customer account notes.
bullets: Risk: private account details may be shared or used in the wrong way.
Risk: the reply may be false, rude, unfair, or unsuitable for the case.
Safeguard: use approved data and limit what the system can access.
Safeguard: require a person to review sensitive or high-impact replies before sending.
screens.callout: Your turn: name one more risk and one simple safeguard. A good safeguard lowers either the chance of harm or the size of the harm.

screens.title: Start with a small task you can undo
screens.lead: Early practice should build good judgment, not just confidence with buttons.
bullets: Choose a low-impact task, such as drafting headings from fictional notes.
Use public, fictional, supplied, or properly approved information.
Decide what a good result must include before you begin.
Check the result against a trusted source or clear standard.
Keep a person responsible for the final use.
screens.callout: Avoid a first task that decides a loan, screens job applicants, sends an unreviewed complaint reply, or changes live business data.

screens.title: Match the capability to the work
screens.lead: AI can support work in several ways. People still set the goal, supply context, check the result, and own the outcome.
rows: What clear conditions should the system follow?
Approve the rules and handle exceptions.
What score, category, or result is being estimated?
Check the data, errors, and impact.
What new content should the system draft?
Check facts, tone, rights, and fit.
Which trusted source should support the answer?
Check that the source is current and useful.
What steps and tools may the system use?
Limit access and approve high-impact steps.
screens.recap_note: Study tip: cover the last two columns. Explain each capability in your own words, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Sort a safe task
screens.lead: Drafting a welcome email is generation. Input: approved event facts. Output: an unsent email. Reviewer: team lead. Stop before sending.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Use one main label for each task. Explain any overlap. Include an input, output, reviewer and stop point for your chosen task.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished the Module 1 lesson
screens.lead: Before you continue, make sure you can explain the ideas below in your own words.
bullets: AI is a group of abilities, not one machine mind.
Rules, prediction, generation, retrieval, and agentic action do different jobs.
A clear answer can still be wrong.
More access and higher impact require stronger checks.
People remain responsible for goals, review, and final decisions.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 2: Prompting, Revision, and Checking Output
modules.description: Clear work orders, CIDI, focused revision, and quality checks.

screens.title: Module 2: Prompting, Revision, and Checking Output
screens.lead: A prompt is the full set of instructions and information you give an AI tool. Good prompts reduce guessing and make answers easier to check.
outcomes: Build a clear prompt.
Use the CIDI framework.
Improve weak output with focused follow-up.
Check and save a prompt that works.
screens.start_body: Create a Tested Prompt and Output Portfolio with the prompt, first answer, checks, changes, and final decision.

screens.title: A prompt is more than a question
screens.lead: Think of a prompt as a work order for a new helper.
bullets: It explains the situation and why the task matters.
It tells the system what action to take.
It sets the format, limits, tone, and quality rules.
It includes the notes, text, or data the system should use.
screens.callout: A longer prompt is not always better. A complete prompt gives the right information for the task.

screens.title: Search words and prompts do different jobs
screens.lead: Both can be useful, but they guide a system in different ways.

sides.title: Search words
items: The user opens and checks sources

sides.title: A full prompt
items: Asks the system to do a task
Best for creating or changing output

screens.title: CIDI gives every prompt four clear parts
screens.lead: Use CIDI to spot what is missing before you run the prompt.

cards.title: Context
cards.body: Why the task matters, who it is for, and what the reader needs.

cards.title: Instruction
cards.body: The action the AI should take.

cards.title: Details
cards.body: Format, tone, length, limits, and success rules.

cards.title: Input
cards.body: The exact notes, text, table, or other source to use.

screens.title: C is for Context
screens.lead: Context helps the tool understand the setting around the task.
bullets: Name the purpose of the work.
Name the audience or user.
Explain what they already know.
State the decision or next step the output should support.
screens.callout: Example: 'This update is for leaders who need a quick, non-technical view of project status.'

screens.title: I is for Instruction
screens.lead: The instruction is the main action word in the prompt.
bullets: Use a clear verb, such as summarize, compare, rewrite, classify, or draft.
Ask for one main job at a time when the task is new.
State what the system must not do.
Do not hide the real task inside a long story.
screens.callout: Example: 'Draft a project update using only the notes below. Do not add facts.'

screens.title: D is for Details
screens.lead: Details describe what a good answer should look like.
bullets: Choose the format, such as bullets, a table, or an email.
Set a useful length.
Name the tone and reading level.
Add boundaries, labels, and facts that must be included.
screens.callout: Example: 'Use five bullets, plain language, and mark missing facts [VERIFY].'

screens.title: I is for Input
screens.lead: Input is the material the system should use.
bullets: Paste or attach only safe, approved material.
Label where the input begins and ends.
Keep facts separate from your instructions.
Tell the system to point out gaps instead of filling them.
screens.callout: Good input cannot guarantee a good answer, but missing or unclear input makes errors more likely.

screens.title: A weak prompt leaves too much to guess
screens.lead: Compare the amount of useful direction in these two requests.

screens.title: Common prompt mistakes
screens.lead: Most weak prompts fail because an important part of the work order is missing.
bullets: Too vague: the system must guess the goal.
Too broad: many jobs are mixed into one request.
No source: the system may use general patterns instead of your facts.
No limits: the answer may be too long, unsafe, or off-topic.
No success rules: you do not know how to judge the result.
screens.callout: Fix the missing part. Do not keep adding random words to the prompt.

screens.title: Worked example: repair a project update
screens.lead: A project lead writes: 'Write an update about the portal project.' The first draft invents a launch date and budget claim.
bullets: Context: non-technical leaders need a short status update.
Instruction: draft from the verified notes only.
Details: five bullets; mark gaps [VERIFY]; do not add dates or costs.
Input: approved navigation; two contrast issues remain; testing starts Monday.
screens.callout: The better prompt reduces guessing. A person must still compare the answer with every source note.

screens.title: Decide what good means before you generate
screens.lead: If you wait until the answer appears, review can become a matter of taste.
bullets: Accuracy: every fact matches the input.
Completeness: required points are present.
Clarity: the reader can understand the message.
Tone: the wording fits the audience.
Usability: the format supports the next step.
screens.callout: Write the criteria first. Then use the same list to judge every version.

screens.title: Use a prompt-output-review-revise loop
screens.lead: Prompting is a cycle, not a one-time command.
bullets: Prompt: give the best complete request you can.
Output: save the first answer.
Review: mark strong parts, errors, gaps, and risks.
Revise: request one focused change or rewrite the prompt.
Decide: use, revise again, or reject the result.
screens.callout: Keep the first answer and your changes. They show how the final result became trustworthy.

screens.title: Three useful ways to critique output
screens.lead: A critique should name the problem and the rule for fixing it.

cards.title: Fact check
cards.body: Link each claim to the source. Mark anything unsupported.

cards.title: Criteria score
cards.body: Score accuracy, completeness, clarity, tone, and use.

cards.title: Red-team check
cards.body: Ask how the answer could fail, confuse, harm, or break a rule.

screens.title: Focused follow-up works better than 'try again'
screens.lead: Tell the system exactly what needs to change and what must stay the same.
bullets: Preserve the verified facts.
Shorten the opening to two sentences.
Add the missing limit.
Turn the list into a table.
Mark every claim that needs proof.
screens.callout: A focused change is easier to review because you know what should be different.

screens.title: Prompt chaining breaks a large task into steps
screens.lead: A prompt chain uses the result of one step as input for the next step.
bullets: Step 1: organize the source notes.
Step 2: create an outline.
Step 3: draft one section.
Step 4: check the section against the source.
Step 5: combine approved parts.
screens.callout: Add a check between steps. An early error can spread through the whole chain.

screens.title: Chaining can improve control or spread errors
screens.lead: The value depends on the checks between steps.

sides.title: Helpful chain
items: A person approves the final result

sides.title: Risky chain
items: The first output is treated as fact
No one checks the combined result

screens.title: A reusable prompt is a maintained work tool
screens.lead: A prompt that worked once is not yet a standard process.
bullets: Record the task and safe input type.
Save the prompt and expected format.
Add the review checklist and known limits.
Name the owner and last test date.
Test it again when the product or task changes.
screens.callout: Keep only prompts that another person can understand, test, and review.

screens.title: Which CIDI part is missing?
screens.lead: Prompt: 'Write three friendly reminder emails. Use fewer than 80 words each.' The system is not given the event facts or dates.
bullets: A. Context
B. Instruction
C. Details
D. Input
screens.callout: Best answer: D. Input. The system needs the approved facts it must use.

screens.title: What is the best follow-up?
screens.lead: The draft uses the right facts, but the opening is too long and formal.
bullets: A. Try again
B. Make it better
C. Keep all facts. Rewrite only the opening in two friendly sentences.
D. Start a different task
screens.callout: Best answer: C. It names the weak part, the change, and what must stay the same.

screens.title: Prompting words to know
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.body: The request and supporting information given to AI.

cards.title: Context
cards.body: The setting, purpose, and audience.

cards.title: Instruction
cards.body: The action the AI is asked to take.

cards.title: Details
cards.body: The format, tone, limits, and quality rules.

cards.title: Input
cards.body: The source material the system should use.

cards.title: Evaluation
cards.body: A planned check against clear criteria.

screens.title: The prompt-to-quality loop
screens.lead: A strong prompt starts the work. Review and revision make the result usable.
rows: What is the task and what does good mean?
Write the goal and criteria first.
What context, action, details, and input are needed?
Build the full CIDI work order.
What is correct, missing, weak, or risky?
Compare the answer with sources and rules.
Name the change and protect correct parts.
Can another person reuse and check it?
Keep the prompt, result, limits, and owner.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: A prompt you can improve
screens.lead: Context: staff need a brief invitation. Instruction: draft the invitation. Details: under 80 words; include date, time, room and what to bring. Input: the checked event facts.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Look for every supplied fact. Remove invented details. Explain one focused revision.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 2
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: A prompt is a complete work order.
CIDI means Context, Instruction, Details, and Input.
Good criteria are written before the answer appears.
Focused follow-up fixes a named weakness.
Reusable prompts need tests, limits, and an owner.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 3: Choosing AI Tools and Models
modules.description: Products, models, access, privacy, risk, and fair comparison.

screens.title: Module 3: Managing AI and Choosing the Right Tool
screens.lead: Choose AI by the task, the information, the risk, and the evidence. Do not choose only by a famous name or a clever demo.
outcomes: Separate provider, product, model, and plan.
Explain how a language model creates text.
Compare tools in a fair way.
Use a privacy and risk check before choosing.
screens.start_body: Create an AI Capability and Tool Selection Guide that records the task, risks, options, checks, and final choice.

screens.title: Start with the job, not the brand
screens.lead: The best-known tool is not always the best fit.
bullets: Name the exact task and needed result.
Classify the information that will be used.
Decide what proof or sources the answer needs.
List the access, controls, and human checks.
Count the full cost before comparing products.
screens.callout: A good choice can be explained without saying, 'Everyone else uses it.'

screens.title: Five layers people often mix up
screens.lead: Keeping these layers separate improves choice, privacy review, and problem solving.

cards.title: Provider
cards.body: The company or group that runs the service.

cards.title: Platform
cards.body: An environment that joins models, tools, and controls.

cards.title: Product
cards.body: The app or service a person uses.

cards.title: Model
cards.body: The trained system that makes part of the output.

cards.title: Plan
cards.body: The access, limits, price, support, and controls for an account.

screens.title: What is a large language model?
screens.lead: A large language model, or LLM, learns patterns from a very large amount of text.
bullets: Text is broken into small pieces called tokens.
Training adjusts many numbers inside the model.
The model learns which token is likely to come next.
Your prompt gives fresh context for the current answer.
The model creates one token after another.
screens.callout: An LLM can create useful language without knowing that every sentence is true.

screens.title: What happens when you select Send
screens.lead: A simple view makes the hidden process easier to understand.

cards.title: 1. Receive
cards.body: The product receives your prompt and allowed files.

cards.title: 2. Represent
cards.body: Text becomes tokens and number patterns.

cards.title: 3. Predict
cards.body: The model estimates useful next tokens.

cards.title: 4. Add tools
cards.body: The product may search, retrieve, calculate, or use code.

cards.title: 5. Return
cards.body: The product shows the output and may include sources or actions.

screens.title: Why language models can hallucinate
screens.lead: A hallucination is a clear-sounding answer that is false, invented, or not supported.
bullets: The model predicts likely language. It does not automatically check a fact book.
A missing detail may be filled with a common pattern.
Old or weak training patterns may shape the answer.
A source can be named even when it does not exist.
A confident tone is not proof.
screens.callout: Ask for sources when needed, open them yourself, and check important claims against trusted evidence.

screens.title: The same prompt can produce different answers
screens.lead: Products and models may use different training, settings, tools, and safety rules.

screens.title: Think in capability groups
screens.lead: A category-first view helps you compare what a system can do before you compare names.
bullets: General assistant: supports many text and thinking tasks.
Embedded assistant: works inside an app such as email or documents.
Special tool: focuses on one job, such as design or transcription.
Developer workflow: joins models, data, tools, and custom controls.
Agentic system: can choose and carry out allowed steps.
screens.callout: One product may fit more than one group. Describe the actual setup you will use.

screens.title: Access changes the level of control needed
screens.lead: Ask what the system can read, create, change, or send.

cards.title: Respond
cards.body: Creates an answer but takes no outside action.

cards.title: Retrieve
cards.body: Reads from allowed sources.

cards.title: Use tools
cards.body: Runs calculators, code, or other connected tools.

cards.title: Create or change
cards.body: Writes files or changes records.

cards.title: Send or act
cards.body: Shares, publishes, buys, deletes, or triggers another action.

screens.title: Capability and access are two different questions
screens.lead: A strong model with no file access may be safer than a weaker model connected to important systems.
bullets: First ask what ability the task needs.
Then ask how the product gets information.
List what it can change or send.
Add controls based on the possible harm.
Give the least access needed for the task.
screens.callout: More ability does not always mean more risk. More access and action can greatly increase risk.

screens.title: Use a privacy traffic light
screens.lead: Classify the information before you open a tool.
bullets: Green: public, fictional, supplied practice, or approved low-risk information.
Yellow: internal information that needs policy and tool approval.
Red: passwords, secret keys, protected records, or highly sensitive material.
Check storage, training use, access, sharing, and deletion rules.
When unsure, stop and ask.
screens.callout: The same product may be fine for a green task and wrong for a red task.

screens.title: A reusable tool-selection checklist
screens.lead: Use the same questions each time a new AI product appears.

cards.title: Task fit
cards.body: Can it produce the result in the form you need?

cards.title: Evidence
cards.body: Can you check sources, calculations, or output?

cards.title: Information
cards.body: Is the tool approved for this data?

cards.title: Controls
cards.body: Are access, review, logs, and approvals strong enough?

cards.title: Workflow
cards.body: Can people use and review it in the real process?

cards.title: Cost
cards.body: What is the full setup and ongoing cost?

screens.title: A plan changes access, not automatic safety
screens.lead: Paid and business plans may add features, support, and controls.
bullets: A paid plan may allow larger files or stronger admin settings.
Data terms may differ by plan or contract.
A feature may be missing in your region or account.
Payment does not prove that private data is approved.
Your organization still decides what use is allowed.
screens.callout: Check the actual plan, settings, contract, and workplace policy before using sensitive information.

screens.title: Compare the task experience, not the slogan
screens.lead: A fair test uses the same harmless task and the same scoring rules.

screens.title: Check current terms before real use
screens.lead: Product names, features, prices, and rules can change.
bullets: Use official product and help pages.
Check the page date and your account settings.
Confirm whether prompts or files may be stored or used.
Check regional limits and supported file types.
Record the date of your decision.
screens.callout: A comparison is a dated decision, not a permanent ranking.

screens.title: Which tool is the better fit?
screens.lead: Tool A gives a polished answer but no sources. Tool B gives a shorter answer with links to the approved policy. The task is to answer a policy question.
bullets: A. Tool A because it sounds better
B. Tool B because the answer can be checked
C. Either one without review
D. The most expensive one
screens.callout: Best answer: B. The task needs source-backed evidence that a person can verify.

screens.title: What should happen first?
screens.lead: A team wants to upload private customer records into a popular AI product.
bullets: A. Test the best model
B. Buy a paid plan
C. Classify the data and check approval and terms
D. Remove the file name only
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Privacy belongs to the task and information, not to the popularity of the brand.

screens.title: Tool-selection words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Provider
cards.body: The company or group that runs a service.

cards.title: Product
cards.body: The app or service a person uses.

cards.title: Model
cards.body: The trained system that produces part of the output.

cards.title: Plan
cards.body: The access level, limits, and controls.

cards.title: Capability
cards.body: What the configured system can do.

cards.title: Hallucination
cards.body: A false or unsupported answer that sounds clear.

screens.title: Choose by task, risk, and evidence
screens.lead: A useful choice can be explained and tested.
rows: Name the job before the tool.
Match ability and access to the task.
How will the result be checked?
Use sources, tests, and clear criteria.
What will the full workflow require?
Count setup, review, support, and risk.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Compare two options
screens.lead: Accuracy: A changes optional attendance to required, so it fails that requirement. B preserves the facts. A fluent sentence can still be wrong.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Use identical input. Mark privacy and cost as unknown if the sample does not supply them; do not invent scores. Use approved tools or compare the supplied samples.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 3
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Provider, platform, product, model, and plan are different layers.
LLMs predict tokens and can sound right while being wrong.
Capability and access must both be checked.
Privacy depends on the task and information.
Fair comparisons use the same input and scoring rules.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 4: AI for Everyday Work
modules.description: Planning, summaries, ideas, and useful first drafts.

screens.title: Module 4: AI for Everyday Work
screens.lead: AI can help with routine planning, organizing, summaries, and first drafts. The person still sets priorities and makes the final choice.
outcomes: Spot routine tasks that fit AI help.
Create useful plans and summaries.
Brainstorm without treating ideas as facts.
Measure whether AI truly improves the work.
screens.start_body: Create an Everyday Work Improvement Pack that compares the task before and after AI help.

screens.title: AI is a fast junior helper
screens.lead: A new helper can organize, suggest, and draft. The helper does not know your whole situation.
bullets: Give the system a clear task and safe input.
Ask for a draft or options, not hidden authority.
Check facts, dates, names, and missing details.
Keep priorities, exceptions, and final choices with a person.
screens.callout: Use AI to reduce friction around the work, not to remove human judgment.

screens.title: Good first tasks share four traits
screens.lead: Routine work is a better starting point when errors are easy to spot and fix.

cards.title: Repeated
cards.body: The task happens often enough for practice to matter.

cards.title: Clear
cards.body: The desired result and format can be explained.

cards.title: Low risk
cards.body: An error is unlikely to harm a person or the business.

cards.title: Easy to review
cards.body: A person can check the answer quickly.

screens.title: Separate assistance from authority
screens.lead: AI can prepare work without owning the decision.

screens.title: Start a summary with a clear purpose
screens.lead: A summary is not just a shorter copy. It should help a certain reader do something.
bullets: Name the reader and what they need to know.
Set the length and format.
List facts that must not be left out.
Tell the system not to add facts.
Compare the summary with the source.
screens.callout: A summary for a manager, a customer, and a technician may need different details.

screens.title: Different summaries serve different needs
screens.lead: Choose the form that fits the reader and the next step.

cards.title: Quick brief
cards.body: Main point, key facts, and next action.

cards.title: Executive summary
cards.body: Purpose, key evidence, risk, and decision needed.

cards.title: Action summary
cards.body: Tasks, owners, results, and due conditions.

cards.title: Study summary
cards.body: Main ideas, examples, terms, and questions.

screens.title: AI can help organize a schedule
screens.lead: A useful schedule shows what must happen, in what order, and where time is tight.
bullets: Give the tasks, dates, time limits, and fixed events.
State which tasks depend on others.
Ask the system to flag conflicts and missing information.
Do not let it invent deadlines or owners.
A person approves the final order.
screens.callout: Scheduling support is useful when the facts are clear. It is risky when missing details are silently guessed.

screens.title: Use AI to turn rough notes into a first plan
screens.lead: A first plan gives you something to review instead of starting from a blank page.
bullets: Group related tasks.
Suggest a sensible order.
Mark urgent items and unknowns.
Add space for owners and due conditions.
Review the plan against real priorities.
screens.callout: The output is a proposal. It becomes the plan only after an accountable person approves it.

screens.title: Brainstorming creates options, not facts
screens.lead: AI can produce many ideas quickly. Some will be weak, repeated, unrealistic, or wrong.
bullets: State the goal and limits before asking for ideas.
Request different types of options.
Do not assume an idea is new or allowed.
Group and score the ideas after generation.
Choose with human judgment and real evidence.
screens.callout: Separate the creative step from the judging step.

screens.title: Everyday uses by role
screens.lead: The same core abilities can support many jobs.

cards.title: Administration
cards.body: Draft checklists, organize notes, and prepare first schedules.

cards.title: Customer service
cards.body: Draft replies from approved facts and policies.

cards.title: Sales
cards.body: Prepare call questions and organize public account research.

cards.title: Operations
cards.body: Summarize issues and suggest categories for review.

cards.title: Managers
cards.body: Compare options and prepare decision questions.

cards.title: Students
cards.body: Build study guides and explain unfamiliar ideas.

screens.title: A safe everyday workflow has four steps
screens.lead: Keep the person active from the start to the finish.
bullets: Capture: begin with safe, useful notes.
Draft: ask AI to organize, summarize, or propose.
Review: correct facts, gaps, tone, and priorities.
Decide: a person chooses the final action.
screens.callout: Saving time on the draft does not remove the need to review the whole result.

screens.title: Measure the whole before-and-after process
screens.lead: A four-minute draft that needs fifteen minutes of repair is not a four-minute workflow.
bullets: Measure preparation time.
Measure generation or task time.
Measure review and correction time.
Record quality, errors, and rework.
Compare the useful final result, not just speed.
screens.callout: Productivity means useful outcomes compared with time, attention, cost, quality, and risk.

screens.title: Good productivity habits and weak habits
screens.lead: Small habits often matter more than special prompt tricks.

screens.title: Know the limits of everyday AI use
screens.lead: AI can make routine work easier, but it can also create extra work or hidden risk.
bullets: A summary may leave out a key exception.
A schedule may invent a deadline.
A plan may miss workplace history or relationships.
A fast draft may use the wrong tone.
Too much AI use can weaken attention and skill.
screens.callout: Use AI where review is easier than creating the first draft from nothing.

screens.title: Is this assistance or authority?
screens.lead: AI turns approved notes into three possible subject lines. A manager chooses one after checking the message.
bullets: A. Assistance
B. Authority
C. A final business decision
D. An unsafe action
screens.callout: Best answer: A. AI creates options, while the manager makes the choice.

screens.title: Did the workflow save time?
screens.lead: Manual work took 20 minutes. AI drafting took 4 minutes and review took 18 minutes.
bullets: A. Yes, it saved 16 minutes
B. Yes, because AI was used
C. No, the reviewed process took 22 minutes
D. There is no need to measure
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Count the full process, including review and correction.

screens.title: Everyday-work words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: First draft
cards.body: A starting version that must be reviewed.

cards.title: Brainstorming
cards.body: Making options before choosing.

cards.title: Summary
cards.body: A shorter version that keeps the main meaning.

cards.title: Constraint
cards.body: A rule or limit the result must follow.

cards.title: Workflow
cards.body: A repeated set of steps and decisions.

cards.title: Productivity
cards.body: Useful results compared with time, cost, quality, and effort.

screens.title: Keep judgment inside the workflow
screens.lead: Everyday AI works best as checked support for a clear task.
rows: Is the task repeated, clear, low risk, and easy to check?
What result, input, format, and limits are needed?
What can AI prepare or suggest?
What facts, gaps, tone, or priorities need correction?
Count time, quality, corrections, and risk.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Check a draft against notes
screens.lead: Bad draft: “A new printer was approved.” Better: “The team is considering a new printer.” This preserves the decision status in the notes.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Keep the count, owner, date and decision status accurate. Do not claim the printer was approved.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 4
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Good first uses are repeated, clear, low risk, and easy to check.
Summaries need a purpose and audience.
Brainstormed ideas are options, not facts.
AI assistance must not quietly become authority.
Measure the complete reviewed workflow.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 5: Workplace Communication
modules.description: Email, reports, plain language, tone, and approval.

screens.title: Module 5: AI for Professional Communication
screens.lead: AI can help turn notes into emails, reports, and plain-language documents. The human author remains responsible for every fact, promise, and effect.
outcomes: Draft messages for a clear audience and purpose.
Turn notes into organized documents.
Protect facts, voice, privacy, and access.
Approve only work you can defend.
screens.start_body: Create a Professional Communication Package with an email, a one-page brief, source checks, and final approval notes.

screens.title: A polished message can still be wrong
screens.lead: Good grammar is only one part of professional communication.
bullets: The facts must match approved sources.
The message must fit the reader and relationship.
The requested action must be clear and allowed.
Private information must be protected.
The accountable author must be willing to sign it.
screens.callout: AI can help build the message. It does not own the promise or the result.

screens.title: Begin with approved source material
screens.lead: Tell the system what information it may use before asking it to write.
bullets: Separate verified facts from guesses and open questions.
Use only approved notes, policy, records, or public sources.
Tell the system not to fill gaps.
Mark missing items [VERIFY].
Keep the source beside the draft during review.
screens.callout: A good-looking draft does not repair missing or unapproved source material.

screens.title: Design the message for its reader
screens.lead: A useful document helps the reader understand and take the right next step.

cards.title: Audience
cards.body: Who will read it and what do they already know?

cards.title: Purpose
cards.body: Why is the message being sent?

cards.title: Action
cards.body: What should the reader do or decide?

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: What level of warmth, care, or formality fits?

cards.title: Format
cards.body: Which structure makes the message easy to use?

cards.title: Limits
cards.body: What must not be promised, shared, or invented?

screens.title: AI can help with email from first draft to revision
screens.lead: Email tasks work best when the prompt includes the relationship and the needed result.
bullets: Give the approved facts and the reason for writing.
Name the reader and tone.
Request a clear subject line and short body.
State the next action and any real deadline.
Review names, dates, links, promises, and attachments.
screens.callout: Never let AI invent a refund, delivery date, approval, or policy promise.

screens.title: Tone changes how facts are received
screens.lead: Keep the facts stable while adjusting the way they are expressed.

screens.title: Reports need structure before full sentences
screens.lead: Ask AI to organize the parts before drafting the whole report.
bullets: Purpose and question
Background and approved facts
Findings or options
Risks, limits, and open questions
Recommendation and next step
screens.callout: An outline makes missing evidence easier to see before polished writing hides the gap.

screens.title: Use a claim-to-source check
screens.lead: Every important statement in a report should have support.
bullets: List each factual claim.
Point to the exact source note, record, or page.
Mark the claim supported, incomplete, or unsupported.
Correct or remove weak claims.
Record who approved the final version.
screens.callout: If you cannot show the source, do not present the claim as a confirmed fact.

screens.title: Plain language makes work easier to use
screens.lead: Plain language is direct and organized. It is not childish.
bullets: Use short sentences and familiar words.
Put the main point first.
Explain needed technical terms.
Break long steps into a list.
Use headings that tell the reader what comes next.
screens.callout: A clear document reduces confusion, questions, and avoidable mistakes.

screens.title: Translation needs more than word replacement
screens.lead: A translated message must keep the meaning, tone, names, numbers, and purpose.
bullets: State the language and audience.
Protect product names and required terms.
Ask for unclear phrases to be flagged.
Use a qualified reviewer when the result has high impact.
Do not assume the most fluent version is the most accurate.
screens.callout: Legal, medical, safety, and official documents need suitable professional review.

screens.title: Choose the tool by the communication task
screens.lead: Different tasks need different features and controls.

cards.title: Short draft
cards.body: A general approved assistant may be enough.

cards.title: Source-based report
cards.body: Use a tool that can work with approved documents and show sources.

cards.title: Team document
cards.body: Use an approved workplace tool with access controls and version history.

cards.title: Sensitive message
cards.body: Use the approved environment and stronger human review.

screens.title: Review through eight lenses
screens.lead: Use a checklist instead of asking only whether the writing sounds good.

cards.title: Facts
cards.body: Names, dates, numbers, and claims match the source.

cards.title: Complete
cards.body: The needed points and limits are present.

cards.title: Audience
cards.body: The reader can understand and act.

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: The voice fits the relationship.

cards.title: Privacy
cards.body: No information is shared without approval.

cards.title: Authority
cards.body: No promise or decision goes beyond the author.

cards.title: Access
cards.body: Headings, contrast, links, and format are usable.

cards.title: Voice
cards.body: The final wording sounds intentional and human.

screens.title: Keep an authentic human voice
screens.lead: AI may smooth every message into the same generic style.
bullets: Restore the words your organization normally uses.
Use the writer's natural level of warmth and directness.
Remove empty phrases and overdone praise.
Keep the message specific to the real situation.
Read it aloud before approval.
screens.callout: The final version should sound like a responsible person, not a machine trying to sound professional.

screens.title: Accessibility is part of communication quality
screens.lead: A message is not complete if the intended reader cannot use it.
bullets: Use clear headings and reading order.
Write useful link text.
Add alt text for meaningful images.
Use readable contrast and font size.
Do not use color as the only way to show meaning.
screens.callout: Accessibility checks belong in the first review, not at the end as an extra.

screens.title: Communication risks can affect real people
screens.lead: AI-assisted words may create promises, harm trust, or expose private information.
bullets: Do not use private details in unapproved tools.
Check for unfair or blaming language.
Do not create fake quotes or approvals.
Review legal, medical, financial, or safety claims with qualified people.
Keep a clear human author and approver.
screens.callout: Responsibility stays with the people who choose, review, approve, and send the message.

screens.title: What is the main problem?
screens.lead: An AI draft politely tells a customer that a refund was approved. The source notes do not mention a refund.
bullets: A. The tone is too friendly
B. The message is too short
C. The draft invented an unauthorized promise
D. The subject line is missing
screens.callout: Best answer: C. A polished promise is still wrong when the source and author do not support it.

screens.title: What should happen before drafting?
screens.lead: A supervisor needs a one-page update from rough project notes.
bullets: A. Ask AI to fill all missing details
B. Separate verified facts, open questions, and limits
C. Choose the longest report style
D. Send the notes to any public tool
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Approved source material and clear gaps should come first.

screens.title: Communication words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Audience
cards.body: The person or group the message is for.

cards.title: Purpose
cards.body: The result the message should support.

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: The feeling and level of formality in the words.

cards.title: Source fidelity
cards.body: Keeping claims true to the source.

cards.title: Plain language
cards.body: Clear, direct writing with familiar words.

cards.title: Accessibility
cards.body: Making content usable by people with different needs.

screens.title: A document is ready when the author can defend it
screens.lead: Writing quality includes facts, purpose, access, privacy, and authority.
rows: What approved facts may be used?
Set audience, purpose, action, and tone.
Request a clear structure and no invented facts.
What could be wrong or harmful?
A person signs and sends only defensible work.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: One message, two audiences
screens.lead: Manager: “Please approve the replacement-part check. The order is delayed two days.” Customer: “Your order is delayed by two days. We will send an update tomorrow at noon.” Neither version promises a refund.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Keep the delay and update time in both versions. Do not invent a resolution or expose internal blame.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 5
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Professional writing needs more than correct grammar.
Start with approved source material.
Design for the reader, purpose, action, and tone.
Check facts, privacy, access, authority, and voice.
The human author owns every promise and effect.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 6: Multimodal and Digital Creation
modules.description: Images, documents, audio, rights, access, and disclosure.

screens.title: Module 6: Multimodal AI and Digital Creation
screens.lead: Multimodal AI can work with text, images, audio, video, charts, scans, and documents. Each type of media needs its own checks.
outcomes: Explain multimodal AI.
Write a clear creative brief.
Inspect media for errors and risk.
Apply rights, access, and disclosure checks.
screens.start_body: Create a Multimodal Content and QA Pack with a brief, draft asset, inspection record, alt text, and disclosure choice.

screens.title: Multimodal means more than text
screens.lead: Some AI products can take in or create several types of media.
bullets: Read text in an image or scan.
Describe or create an image.
Turn audio into a transcript.
Read a chart or table.
Join text, images, sound, and files in one task.
screens.callout: More media creates more ways to help and more ways to make mistakes.

screens.title: Each medium can fail in a different way
screens.lead: The review method must fit the type of content.

cards.title: Images
cards.body: Objects, hands, logos, and text may look wrong.

cards.title: Audio
cards.body: Speakers, names, or numbers may be confused.

cards.title: Documents
cards.body: Text, tables, or page order may be missed.

cards.title: Charts
cards.body: Labels, scales, or data meaning may be read incorrectly.

cards.title: Video
cards.body: A realistic scene may show something that never happened.

screens.title: A creative brief sets the direction
screens.lead: Write the communication need before you ask for an image or design.
bullets: Audience: who should notice and understand it?
Purpose: what message or action matters?
Format: where will the asset be used?
Style: what should it feel like?
Rules: what must be included, avoided, or approved?
screens.callout: A clear brief keeps the goal more important than the novelty of the generator.

screens.title: Turn the brief into an image prompt
screens.lead: An image prompt should describe what to show and what to avoid.
bullets: Name the main subject and action.
Describe the setting, layout, and point of view.
Set the style, color, and mood.
Leave safe space for text when needed.
List banned logos, private people, unsafe details, or unwanted text.
screens.callout: Generate the image without important words inside it when accurate spelling is required. Add final text in a design tool.

screens.title: Inspect a generated image in passes
screens.lead: Slow down and check one type of problem at a time.

cards.title: Meaning
cards.body: Does the image support the brief and audience?

cards.title: Objects
cards.body: Are people, hands, tools, and places believable?

cards.title: Text
cards.body: Are words, signs, labels, and numbers correct?

cards.title: Rights
cards.body: Are logos, brands, likenesses, and source material allowed?

cards.title: Access
cards.body: Is there clear contrast and useful alt text?

cards.title: Risk
cards.body: Could the image mislead someone about a real event?

screens.title: Text inside AI images often needs repair
screens.lead: Image systems may draw letters as shapes instead of creating dependable text.
bullets: Check every word, date, price, and contact detail.
Do not trust a readable-looking sign at a glance.
Keep important text outside the generated image when possible.
Add final wording with normal design software.
Review the finished layout again.
screens.callout: A beautiful flyer with the wrong date is still a failed flyer.

screens.title: Uploaded documents still need page-by-page checks
screens.lead: An AI tool may miss text, tables, footnotes, handwriting, or page order.
bullets: Confirm that all pages were received.
Compare extracted text with the page image.
Check table headings, rows, and units.
Look for notes, stamps, and small print.
Use OCR results as a draft, not proof.
screens.callout: For important documents, inspect both the extracted content and the visible page.

screens.title: Audio and transcripts can confuse speakers
screens.lead: Speech tools may mishear names, numbers, accents, or overlapping voices.
bullets: Get consent before recording or processing a meeting.
Check who said each important statement.
Verify names, dates, amounts, and decisions.
Mark unclear sections instead of guessing.
Follow rules for storage, sharing, and deletion.
screens.callout: A transcript is a helpful draft record. It is not an automatic official record.

screens.title: Charts need the data behind them
screens.lead: A chart image can look clear while showing the wrong scale or meaning.
bullets: Check the title and labels.
Check the units and time period.
Check the axis and starting point.
Compare plotted values with the table.
Ask what data is missing or hidden.
screens.callout: Do not approve a chart only because the picture looks professional.

screens.title: Synthetic media can inform or mislead
screens.lead: Synthetic media is content created or changed with generative tools.

sides.title: Harmful use
items: Fake evidence of a real event
A person's likeness used without consent
False audio or video spreads as news
A brand or source is copied without permission

screens.title: Deepfakes make verification more important
screens.lead: A deepfake is realistic-looking media that changes or invents a person's face, voice, or actions.
bullets: Do not rely on realism alone.
Find the original source and date.
Check trusted reports or official channels.
Look for cuts, missing context, and unusual details.
Pause before sharing urgent or emotional content.
screens.callout: The safest response to shocking media is often to stop, verify, and avoid spreading it.

screens.title: Permission to use a tool is not permission to use every input
screens.lead: Rights and privacy still apply when AI is involved.
bullets: Check copyright and licence terms.
Check trademarks and brand rules.
Get consent for private people, voices, or likenesses.
Do not upload confidential source material without approval.
Keep a record of sources, prompts, edits, and approvals.
screens.callout: When rights are unclear, use original, licensed, public-domain, supplied, or properly approved material.

screens.title: Provenance tells the story of the media
screens.lead: Provenance is information about where content came from and how it changed.
bullets: Record the source file or brief.
Save the prompt and key settings.
Record major edits and added text.
Name the reviewer and approval date.
Keep the final disclosure choice.
screens.callout: A useful record helps another person understand and check the asset later.

screens.title: Use disclosure when AI help matters to the audience
screens.lead: Disclosure means telling people about important AI creation or changes.
bullets: Disclose when rules or policy require it.
Disclose when realistic media could confuse people.
Disclose material changes to a real person, event, or claim.
Use clear words near the content.
Do not hide the notice in hard-to-find text.
screens.callout: A disclosure should help the audience understand what was created or changed.

screens.title: Accessibility is part of the first design
screens.lead: Build access into the asset before it is published.
bullets: Write useful alt text for meaningful images.
Use readable contrast and type size.
Provide captions or transcripts for audio and video.
Keep a clear reading order.
Do not use color as the only sign of meaning.
screens.callout: Alt text should explain the useful meaning, not list every pixel.

screens.title: What should the learner do first?
screens.lead: An AI image contains the event title, date, and phone number inside the picture.
bullets: A. Publish because it looks clear
B. Check every word and add final text in a design tool
C. Make the colors brighter
D. Remove the alt text
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Generated image text is not dependable and must be checked or replaced.

screens.title: Is a transcript an official record?
screens.lead: A meeting transcript lists the wrong person as approving a payment.
bullets: A. Yes, because AI created it
B. Yes, if the file is long
C. No, important statements and speakers must be verified
D. No one needs to review it
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Transcripts can confuse speakers and words.

screens.title: Digital-creation words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Multimodal
cards.body: Able to work with more than one type of media.

cards.title: Creative brief
cards.body: The audience, purpose, message, format, and limits.

cards.title: Provenance
cards.body: A record of where media came from and how it changed.

cards.title: Alt text
cards.body: A useful text description of an image.

cards.title: Synthetic media
cards.body: Media created or greatly changed by AI.

cards.title: Disclosure
cards.body: A clear notice about important AI help.

screens.title: Inspect the media, not just the prompt
screens.lead: Every medium needs checks that fit its risks.
rows: Set audience, purpose, form, style, and rules.
What may AI generate or read?
Use safe, allowed input and a clear prompt.
What could be wrong in this medium?
Check text, details, source, and context.
What rights, privacy, or consent apply?
Use approved material and keep records.
What access and disclosure are needed?
Add alt text, captions, and a clear notice.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Create and check a clear asset
screens.lead: A useful text alternative is: “Optional staff workshop, 12 October, 10 am, Room B. Bring a laptop.” The event facts matter more than decorative shapes.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Check all dates, text and required items. Provide a text alternative. If a media tool is unavailable, submit a text layout and annotate how it meets the brief.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 6
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Multimodal AI works across several types of media.
A creative brief sets the goal and limits.
Images, audio, documents, and charts need different checks.
Rights, consent, provenance, access, and disclosure matter.
A person inspects the final asset before use.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 7: Research and Evidence
modules.description: Questions, sources, evidence, citations, and limits.

screens.title: Module 7: AI for Search, Research, and Evidence
screens.lead: AI can help plan research and organize notes. The original source, not the chatbot, remains the authority.
outcomes: Turn a broad topic into a clear question.
Find strong original sources.
Check claims, dates, and support.
Write a brief with useful citations and honest limits.
screens.start_body: Create a Source-Backed Research Brief with a clear question, claim-evidence table, citations, and limitations.

screens.title: AI can be a guide, not the evidence
screens.lead: A guide can point to a useful shelf in a library. The guide is not the book on the shelf.
bullets: Use AI to define terms and plan searches.
Use it to organize sources and find missing questions.
Open the original source yourself.
Read the exact section that supports the claim.
Base conclusions on evidence, not chatbot memory.
screens.callout: A source-backed answer shows where each important claim came from.

screens.title: Make the research question answerable
screens.lead: A clear question makes good sources easier to find.
bullets: State the claim or decision you need to support.
Name the place or group involved.
Set a useful date range.
Define words that could mean different things.
Choose what will be compared.
screens.callout: Broad: 'Is walking good?' Clearer: 'What do public health agencies say about regular walking for adults from 2021 to 2026?'

screens.title: Use a source ladder
screens.lead: Move closer to the original evidence as the claim becomes more important.

cards.title: Primary source
cards.body: Original data, law, policy, research paper, record, or direct statement.

cards.title: Authoritative source
cards.body: An official body or qualified organization responsible for the topic.

cards.title: Strong secondary source
cards.body: A careful explanation that links to original evidence.

cards.title: Weak lead
cards.body: A post or summary with no clear source. It may help you search, but not prove the claim.

screens.title: Primary and secondary sources have different jobs
screens.lead: Both may be useful when their roles are clear.

sides.title: Primary or authoritative
items: Shows the original rule, data, or finding

sides.title: Secondary
items: Should link back to original evidence

screens.title: Build search queries from the question
screens.lead: Good search words name the claim, source type, place, and time.
bullets: Use the main topic and a clear result word.
Add a source type such as report, data, guidance, law, or study.
Add the country, agency, group, or date range.
Try related words when the first search is too broad.
Record which query found useful evidence.
screens.callout: AI can suggest search terms. You still judge the source and open it yourself.

screens.title: Do not accept a citation because it looks real
screens.lead: AI can invent titles, authors, dates, links, and page numbers.
bullets: Open the link or find the source by title.
Check the author or publisher.
Check the date and version.
Read the exact section used.
Confirm that it truly supports the claim.
screens.callout: A correctly formatted citation can still point to the wrong or nonexistent source.

screens.title: A claim-evidence table keeps research honest
screens.lead: Link each important statement to something another person can inspect.
bullets: Claim: the statement you may include.
Source: the original page, paper, record, or dataset.
Exact support: the part that backs the claim.
Status: supported, incomplete, contradicted, or not found.
Limit: what the source does not prove.
screens.callout: Build the table before writing the polished brief.

screens.title: Check every source with four questions
screens.lead: A famous source can still be wrong for your exact claim.

cards.title: Relevant?
cards.body: Does it answer this question and apply to this group or place?

cards.title: Current?
cards.body: Is the date recent enough for the topic?

cards.title: Direct?
cards.body: Does it show the evidence or only repeat someone else?

cards.title: Enough?
cards.body: Does it support the full claim or only part of it?

screens.title: Read around a quote or number
screens.lead: A small extract can lose the condition that changes its meaning.
bullets: Read the heading and nearby paragraphs.
Check notes, units, and definitions.
Look for exceptions and warnings.
Check the sample size and time period when data is used.
Do not stretch a narrow finding into a broad promise.
screens.callout: Context is part of the evidence.

screens.title: Separate evidence, meaning, and advice
screens.lead: These three layers should not be blended into one confident sentence.
bullets: Evidence: what the source directly shows.
Interpretation: what the evidence may mean.
Recommendation: what someone may choose to do.
Uncertainty: what is still unknown.
Decision: what an accountable person approves.
screens.callout: A source can support evidence without proving your recommendation is the only right choice.

screens.title: Compare options with the same criteria
screens.lead: AI can help build a table, but it should not hide the evidence behind each score.
bullets: Choose the criteria before comparing.
Use the same date and scope for each option.
Link every important claim to a source.
Keep facts separate from preferences.
Show missing information instead of giving a false score.
screens.callout: A neat comparison is only as sound as its sources and rules.

screens.title: Sources may disagree
screens.lead: A conflict does not always mean one source is dishonest.
bullets: Check whether they studied different groups or dates.
Compare how key terms were defined.
Look at methods, sample size, and limits.
Give more weight to stronger and more direct evidence.
Explain the conflict instead of hiding it.
screens.callout: When evidence is mixed, the answer should sound mixed too.

screens.title: Research ethics includes fair use of information
screens.lead: Good research protects people and represents sources honestly.
bullets: Do not upload private or restricted documents without approval.
Do not copy long passages and present them as your own.
Do not remove context that weakens your claim.
Include evidence that challenges your first view.
State who funded or produced a source when it matters.
screens.callout: The goal is a fair answer, not a pile of links that supports only what you hoped to find.

screens.title: Write limitations where readers can see them
screens.lead: Limits help another person judge how much confidence to place in the answer.
bullets: State the date range and location.
Name missing data or weak sources.
Explain when findings may not apply.
Separate current facts from older background.
List questions that still need an expert or better source.
screens.callout: Honest limits make a research brief stronger, not weaker.

screens.title: A free verification habit
screens.lead: For every important claim, pause before you use it.
bullets: Find the original source.
Open it.
Read the relevant part.
Check the date and scope.
Record what it supports and what it does not.
screens.callout: This habit costs little and prevents many confident research errors.

screens.title: Which source is strongest?
screens.lead: You need the current rule for renewing a business licence.
bullets: A. An old social media post
B. A blog that names no source
C. The current page from the issuing government office
D. A chatbot answer with no link
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Use the current original or authoritative source for an important rule.

screens.title: Does the citation prove the claim?
screens.lead: A report says 60% of 100 surveyed users liked a feature. The draft says 60% of all customers will buy it.
bullets: A. Yes, the number is the same
B. No, the draft stretches the sample and changes the claim
C. Yes, because a report exists
D. No source is needed
screens.callout: Best answer: B. The source does not prove a result for all customers or future buying.

screens.title: Research words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Primary source
cards.body: The original data, rule, record, or research.

cards.title: Secondary source
cards.body: An explanation based on other sources.

cards.title: Claim
cards.body: A statement that needs support.

cards.title: Evidence
cards.body: Information that directly supports or tests a claim.

cards.title: Citation
cards.body: Details that help another person find the source.

cards.title: Limitation
cards.body: A reason the conclusion should not be broader or stronger.

screens.title: Keep the source as the authority
screens.lead: AI may guide and organize research, but evidence carries the claim.
rows: What exactly needs to be answered?
Set scope, terms, place, group, and date.
Where is the original evidence likely to be?
Use a source ladder and focused queries.
Does the source support the claim?
Open, read, date, and check context.
What is evidence, meaning, and advice?
Can another person inspect the work?
Use citations, a claim table, and visible limits.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Trace claims to sources
screens.lead: Supported: “12 staff registered” → source B. Not supported: “Everyone will attend.” Inference: “At the time of source B, six seats may remain,” assuming no new registrations.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Use both supplied sources. Separate source facts from your inference. For independent research, use current sources you can open and inspect.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 7
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: A chatbot is not the source.
Clear questions lead to better searches.
Important claims need original or authoritative evidence.
Citations must be opened and checked.
A strong brief separates evidence, meaning, advice, and limits.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 8: Data and Decisions
modules.description: Clean tables, formulas, charts, and sound decisions.

screens.title: Module 8: AI for Spreadsheets, Data, and Decisions
