screens.lead: AI can help inspect tables, suggest formulas, explain patterns, and draft charts. The numbers still need careful checks.
outcomes: Prepare a table before analysis.
Check formulas, units, and missing values.
Choose charts that tell the truth.
Separate evidence from advice.
screens.start_body: Create a checked data summary with a clean table, two useful measures, one chart, and a short decision note.

screens.title: Good analysis begins before the math
screens.lead: A neat answer cannot repair unclear or unreliable data.
bullets: State the question first.
Find where the data came from.
Check what each row and column means.
Look for missing, repeated, or unusual values.
Record changes instead of silently fixing the table.
screens.callout: Prepare the evidence before asking AI to explain it.

screens.title: Two common kinds of data
screens.lead: Knowing the form helps you choose the right tool.

sides.title: Unstructured data
items: Meaning may be hidden in context

screens.title: Give every column one clear meaning
screens.lead: A strong table has a simple rule: one row is one item, and one column is one field.
bullets: Use clear headings.
Keep dates in one format.
Keep money in one currency.
Do not mix totals with detail rows.
Keep notes away from number fields.
screens.callout: Example: Quantity and Unit Price should be separate columns, not one cell that says '4 at $12.'

screens.title: Find common data problems
screens.lead: Mark each problem before you decide how to handle it.

cards.title: Missing
cards.body: A value is blank or was not collected.

cards.title: Duplicate
cards.body: The same record may appear more than once.

cards.title: Wrong type
cards.body: Text appears where a date or number should be.

cards.title: Outlier
cards.body: A value is far from the others and needs review.

cards.title: Mixed units
cards.body: Values use different currencies, times, or measures.

cards.title: Unclear label
cards.body: A heading does not explain what the value means.

screens.title: Do not guess what a blank means
screens.lead: A blank could mean zero, not known, not asked, or not allowed.
bullets: Ask the data owner when possible.
Keep blank and zero separate.
Do not invent a value just to complete the table.
State how many values are missing.
Explain how missing data may change the result.
screens.callout: Missing information is part of the finding.

screens.title: Keep a simple issue log
screens.lead: An issue log makes cleaning work visible and repeatable.
bullets: Name the row or field.
Describe the problem.
Record the change or decision.
Name who approved it when needed.
Keep the original data safe.
screens.callout: A clean table without a record of changes is hard to trust.

screens.title: Use a safe cleaning order
screens.lead: Work from meaning to format, then to calculation.
bullets: Copy the source and protect the original.
Define rows, columns, units, and dates.
Remove confirmed duplicates.
Correct approved formats and labels.
Review missing values and outliers.
Run checks before analysis.
screens.callout: Never let an AI tool overwrite the only copy of your data.

screens.title: A formula must match the business question
screens.lead: Correct arithmetic can still answer the wrong question.
bullets: Name the measure in plain words.
Check the range of cells.
Check the numerator and denominator.
Check units, signs, and rounding.
Test the formula with a small example you can solve yourself.
screens.callout: If you cannot explain the formula, do not use its result in a decision.

screens.title: Use simple measures with care
screens.lead: Each measure answers a different question.

cards.title: Total
cards.body: How much is there altogether?

cards.title: Count
cards.body: How many records meet the rule?

cards.title: Average
cards.body: What is the total divided by the count?

cards.title: Rate
cards.body: What share of the whole meets a condition?

cards.title: Change
cards.body: How much did a value rise or fall?

cards.title: Range
cards.body: How far apart are the smallest and largest values?

screens.title: Check results in a second way
screens.lead: Independent checks catch quiet errors.
bullets: Recalculate a sample by hand.
Compare totals before and after cleaning.
Use a second formula or tool.
Filter the rows behind an unusual result.
Ask whether the answer is possible in the real world.
screens.callout: A matching second check raises confidence. It does not remove the need for judgment.

screens.title: Choose a chart for the question
screens.lead: A chart should make the pattern easier to see, not merely look impressive.

cards.title: Bar
cards.body: Compare amounts across groups.

cards.title: Line
cards.body: Show change across time.

cards.title: Scatter
cards.body: Look for a relationship between two number fields.

cards.title: Table
cards.body: Show exact values when precision matters.

screens.title: Charts can mislead
screens.lead: Small design choices can make a weak change look large or hide an important difference.
bullets: Label axes and units.
Use a fair scale.
Keep time periods even.
Avoid unnecessary 3D shapes.
Show missing data and important notes.
Do not hide groups that weaken the story.
screens.callout: The chart must tell the same truth as the table.

screens.title: Separate fact, meaning, and recommendation
screens.lead: A decision note should show how the conclusion was built.
bullets: Fact: what the checked data shows.
Interpretation: what the pattern may mean.
Recommendation: what action may help.
Uncertainty: what is still unknown.
Owner: who decides and follows up.
screens.callout: AI may suggest an explanation. Treat it as a possibility until evidence supports it.

screens.title: Compare options with the same rules
screens.lead: A fair comparison uses the same measures, period, and assumptions for every option.
bullets: Choose criteria before scoring.
Explain each weight.
Link scores to data.
Show unknown values.
Test how the result changes when an assumption changes.
screens.callout: A score is a tool for discussion, not an automatic decision.

screens.title: Which step comes first?
screens.lead: A table contains mixed currencies, missing dates, and repeated rows.
bullets: A. Ask AI for a chart
B. Clean and define the data
C. Write the recommendation
D. Hide the problem rows
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Define and clean the data before analysis.

screens.title: Can this result be trusted?
screens.lead: AI gives a 17% increase, but nobody checked the formula range or source rows.
bullets: A. Yes, because it is exact
B. Yes, because AI calculated it
C. Not yet; verify the formula and evidence
D. Round it to 20%
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Exact-looking numbers still need checks.

screens.title: Data and decision words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Dataset
cards.body: A collection of related information.

cards.title: Field
cards.body: One type of information in a table column.

cards.title: Outlier
cards.body: A value far from most other values.

cards.title: Formula
cards.body: A rule used to calculate a result.

cards.title: Denominator
cards.body: The whole or base used in a fraction or rate.

cards.title: Assumption
cards.body: Something treated as true for the analysis.

screens.title: Turn data into a checked decision note
screens.lead: Good analysis is a chain of visible choices.
rows: Check fields, units, blanks, repeats, and outliers.
Does the formula answer the question?
Does the chart tell the same truth?
Use clear labels and fair scales.
Separate facts, meaning, advice, and uncertainty.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Clean a small dataset
screens.lead: The three known genuine amounts total 60 and average 20. Do not turn the missing amount into zero. Report: “Known sales total 60; one order amount is missing.”
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Remove only the confirmed duplicate. Preserve the unknown as missing. Test the calculation on the known values and explain limits.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 8
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Prepare the table before analysis.
Never guess what missing data means.
Check formulas and units in a second way.
Choose charts for the question.
Keep evidence separate from advice.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 9: Meetings and Coordination
modules.description: Agendas, notes, decisions, owners, and follow-through.

screens.title: Module 9: AI for Productivity, Meetings, and Work Coordination
screens.lead: AI can help people prepare, capture, organize, and follow up. A meeting only creates value when people know what happens next.
outcomes: Plan a focused meeting.
Use recording and transcription with care.
Separate decisions from discussion.
Create action items that can be checked.
screens.start_body: Create a meeting pack with an agenda, checked notes, a decision log, and clear action items.

screens.title: Begin with the result
screens.lead: A meeting is not the goal. The goal is a decision, plan, shared understanding, or completed action.
bullets: State why the meeting is needed.
Name the result to leave with.
Invite only people who have a role.
Share useful material before the meeting.
Cancel or shorten meetings that can be handled another way.
screens.callout: A clear purpose helps AI draft a useful agenda instead of a list of vague topics.

screens.title: Build an agenda people can use
screens.lead: Each item should tell participants what they must do.
bullets: Name the topic.
State whether it is for information, discussion, or decision.
Assign an owner.
Set a time limit.
List any pre-reading or evidence.
screens.callout: Example: Decide the launch date - owner: Maya - 10 minutes - review the risk list first.

screens.title: Recording requires permission
screens.lead: Audio, video, and transcripts may contain private or restricted information.
bullets: Follow workplace policy and local rules.
Tell people what will be recorded and why.
Get required consent before recording.
Limit who can access the file.
Set a safe storage and deletion period.
screens.callout: If consent or policy is unclear, take approved manual notes instead.

screens.title: A safe AI meeting flow
screens.lead: People stay responsible at every stage.

cards.title: Prepare
cards.body: Draft the purpose, agenda, questions, and pre-read.

cards.title: Capture
cards.body: Record or transcribe only with approval.

cards.title: Organize
cards.body: Separate notes, decisions, actions, and open questions.

cards.title: Verify
cards.body: A person checks names, facts, meaning, and commitments.

cards.title: Share
cards.body: Send the approved record to the right people.

cards.title: Follow up
cards.body: Track actions and close the loop.

screens.title: Discussion is not a decision
screens.lead: A summary must not turn an idea into an approved commitment.

sides.title: Discussion or suggestion
items: Use words such as considered or suggested

sides.title: Decision
items: The group or decision owner approved it
The date and conditions are known

screens.title: Write action items that can be checked
screens.lead: An action item needs more than a verb.
bullets: Owner: one person accountable for the next move.
Result: the thing that will be produced or completed.
Due point: a date, time, or clear condition.
Evidence: how completion will be shown.
Dependency: what must happen first.
screens.callout: Weak: 'Follow up.' Strong: 'Nia sends the approved price list to the sales team by Friday at 3:00 p.m.'

screens.title: Mark uncertainty instead of filling gaps
screens.lead: Transcripts can miss words, speakers, numbers, and decisions.
bullets: Use [VERIFY] beside uncertain text.
Check important names and figures.
Ask the decision owner to confirm commitments.
Do not invent a due date.
Keep open questions separate from actions.
screens.callout: A visible gap is safer than a polished mistake.

screens.title: Create a small decision log
screens.lead: A decision log helps teams remember what changed and why.
bullets: Decision made.
Decision owner.
Date and meeting.
Reason or evidence.
Conditions, limits, or review date.
screens.callout: The log is especially useful when a later meeting revisits the same issue.

screens.title: Check before sending notes
screens.lead: Meeting notes may affect work, money, customers, or staff.
bullets: Check attendee and speaker names.
Check dates, amounts, and deadlines.
Confirm decisions with the right owner.
Remove private details that do not belong.
Use the approved sharing channel.
screens.callout: A fast summary is not finished until a responsible person reviews it.

screens.title: Share only what each person needs
screens.lead: A full transcript is often more sensitive and less useful than approved notes.
bullets: Send a short summary to the wider group.
Limit the transcript to approved users.
Keep private side discussions out of broad notes.
Use clear file names and versions.
Delete recordings according to policy.
screens.callout: Useful access is limited access.

screens.title: Close the loop
screens.lead: Productivity improves when actions return to the team as visible results.
bullets: Track open actions in one place.
Send reminders at a useful time.
Raise blocked items early.
Record completion evidence.
Carry unresolved items into the next agenda.
screens.callout: An AI reminder can help, but the owner remains responsible.

screens.title: Use AI to coordinate, not to create noise
screens.lead: Automation should reduce repeated work without filling inboxes and calendars with low-value output.
bullets: Choose one clear source of truth.
Use standard names and statuses.
Set rules for reminders.
Stop duplicate notices.
Review whether the workflow actually saves time.
screens.callout: More messages do not always mean better coordination.

screens.title: A simple daily productivity pattern
screens.lead: Use AI at small, clear points in the day.
bullets: Morning: organize priorities from approved tasks.
Before work: draft a checklist or first outline.
During work: summarize safe material and track questions.
After work: check results and record the next action.
End of day: remove or store sensitive material correctly.
screens.callout: Keep private or restricted data out of unapproved tools.

screens.title: Is this an action item?
screens.lead: The notes say, 'The team should look at training soon.'
bullets: A. Yes, it is complete
B. No, it needs an owner, result, and due point
C. Yes, because the team was named
D. No meeting notes are needed
screens.callout: Best answer: B. The statement is only a general suggestion.

screens.title: What should happen before recording?
screens.lead: A meeting may include employee and customer details.
bullets: A. Record quietly
B. Ask AI after the meeting
C. Follow policy and get required consent
D. Share the transcript with everyone
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Permission and safe handling come first.

screens.title: Meeting and coordination words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Agenda
cards.body: A plan for the meeting.

cards.title: Transcript
cards.body: A written record of spoken words.

cards.title: Decision log
cards.body: A record of approved choices and their reasons.

cards.title: Action item
cards.body: A task with an owner and clear result.

cards.title: Dependency
cards.body: Something that must happen before another task can finish.

cards.title: Retention
cards.body: How long information is kept.

screens.title: Make meetings lead to action
screens.lead: A useful meeting record is clear, checked, and safe to share.
rows: Name the result before writing the agenda.
Follow policy and gain required consent.
Separate notes, decisions, actions, and questions.
Track owners, due points, evidence, and blockers.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Build an action log
screens.lead: Action: Mina — check shelf list — Thursday. Open decision: printer purchase. Pat will ask finance by Friday; the transcript does not approve a purchase.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Keep suggestions separate from decisions. Check owners and dates. Do not add attendees or approvals that are absent from the transcript.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 9
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Plan meetings around a result.
Record only with approval.
Do not turn discussion into a decision.
Give every action an owner and due point.
Verify and share the right level of detail.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 10: Business Adoption and ROI
modules.description: Processes, pilots, value, full cost, and change.

screens.title: Module 10: AI Across Business - Processes, Adoption, and ROI
screens.lead: A useful AI project begins with a business problem, not a new tool. A small pilot can test value before a larger change.
outcomes: Map a real process.
Choose a small pilot with clear limits.
Measure cost, benefit, and risk.
Plan training, trust, and adoption.
screens.start_body: Create a one-page AI pilot plan with a process map, baseline, measures, safeguards, and decision rule.

screens.title: Start with the problem
screens.lead: Buying a tool before understanding the work can add cost and confusion.
bullets: Name the repeated problem.
Identify who feels the problem.
Describe the current result.
Estimate its time, cost, delay, or error.
Ask whether a non-AI fix may be simpler.
screens.callout: The question is not 'Where can we add AI?' It is 'What result needs to improve?'

screens.title: A process is more than a task list
screens.lead: A process shows how work moves from a trigger to an outcome.
bullets: Trigger: what starts the work.
Input: what information or material arrives.
Steps: what people and systems do.
Decision: where the path can change.
Handoff: where work moves to someone else.
Output and owner: what is delivered and who is accountable.
screens.callout: Include exceptions. The unusual cases often carry the most risk.

screens.title: Observe the real process
screens.lead: The written procedure and the daily process may not match.
bullets: Talk with people who do the work.
Watch several normal cases.
Include busy periods and exceptions.
Record delays, repeated entry, and rework.
Do not blame people for working around a broken step.
screens.callout: Good adoption includes the people who understand the work.

screens.title: Set a baseline
screens.lead: A baseline is the starting measure used for comparison.
bullets: Choose the measure before the pilot.
Use a normal and useful time period.
Record volume and variation.
Include quality and risk, not only speed.
State where the data came from.
screens.callout: Without a baseline, improvement becomes a feeling instead of a measured result.

screens.title: Choose balanced measures
screens.lead: One number rarely tells the whole story.

cards.title: Time
cards.body: Minutes, wait time, or completion time.

cards.title: Cost
cards.body: Labour, tools, setup, support, and rework.

cards.title: Quality
cards.body: Accuracy, completeness, or first-time success.

cards.title: Risk
cards.body: Privacy, security, fairness, or business harm.

cards.title: Experience
cards.body: Effect on customers and staff.

cards.title: Adoption
cards.body: Whether people can and will use the process correctly.

screens.title: A pilot is a controlled test
screens.lead: A pilot tests one idea in a limited setting before a larger rollout.
bullets: Use one clear use case.
Limit the users and data.
Set a start and end date.
Keep a human approval step.
Define what success, failure, and stop mean.
screens.callout: A pilot should be small enough to learn safely and real enough to teach you something useful.

screens.title: Set boundaries before the test
screens.lead: Clear limits prevent a small trial from quietly becoming a risky production system.
bullets: Allowed users and roles.
Allowed and forbidden data.
Allowed actions.
Required reviews and approvals.
Storage, access, and deletion rules.
Who can stop the pilot.
screens.callout: Write the boundaries where every participant can see them.

screens.title: Use thresholds and stop rules
screens.lead: Decide how the team will respond before results arrive.
bullets: Minimum quality level.
Maximum error or complaint rate.
Maximum allowed cost.
Conditions that pause the test.
Conditions that end the test.
Who reviews the evidence.
screens.callout: Pre-set rules reduce the urge to excuse a weak result because people like the tool.

screens.title: Count the full cost
screens.lead: The subscription price is only one part of the cost.
bullets: Licences and usage fees.
Setup and integration.
Training and support.
Human review time.
Security, legal, and compliance work.
Maintenance, monitoring, and corrections.
screens.callout: Also count the cost of leaving the problem unchanged.

screens.title: Name benefits that can be tested
screens.lead: A benefit should connect to a business result.
bullets: Time saved on a repeated step.
Fewer avoidable errors.
Faster customer response.
More consistent documents.
Better access to useful information.
More capacity for higher-value work.
screens.callout: Do not count the same benefit twice under different names.

screens.title: ROI is a comparison, not a promise
screens.lead: A simple return on investment estimate compares net benefit with total cost.
bullets: Estimated benefit minus total cost gives net benefit.
Net benefit divided by total cost gives a simple ROI rate.
Use the same time period for cost and benefit.
Show assumptions and ranges.
Replace estimates with pilot evidence when available.
screens.callout: If benefits are uncertain, show a low, expected, and high case.

screens.title: Risk and value belong on the same page
screens.lead: A faster process may still be a bad change if it creates serious harm.
bullets: List privacy and security risks.
Check unfair effects on people.
Consider customer and employee experience.
Plan what happens when the output is wrong.
Keep accountable people in important decisions.
screens.callout: A good pilot tests whether value can be gained within safe limits.

screens.title: Adoption is a people change
screens.lead: A tool does not create value if people do not understand, trust, or use the process correctly.
bullets: Explain the problem and purpose.
Invite feedback from affected workers.
Train people on both use and limits.
Give support during the change.
Reward honest reporting of errors and concerns.
screens.callout: Do not hide job or workload concerns behind technical language.

screens.title: Build a small adoption playbook
screens.lead: Turn the pilot into a repeatable way of working.

cards.title: Owner
cards.body: Who is accountable for the process?

cards.title: Procedure
cards.body: What steps and approvals are required?

cards.title: Training
cards.body: What must each role know and practise?

cards.title: Support
cards.body: Where do users report questions and problems?

cards.title: Monitoring
cards.body: Which quality, risk, and value measures continue?

cards.title: Review
cards.body: When will the team improve, pause, or stop?

screens.title: Policy turns values into rules
screens.lead: A short AI policy helps people make steady choices.
bullets: Approved and unapproved tools.
Data that may or may not be entered.
Required human review.
Disclosure and record rules.
Security and incident reporting.
Consequences and help channels.
screens.callout: Policy should be clear enough to use during real work.

screens.title: Small businesses can begin small
screens.lead: A limited use case can teach valuable lessons without a large budget.
bullets: Draft common messages with review.
Organize public product information.
Summarize approved notes.
Prepare simple content options.
Test one repeated back-office step.
screens.callout: Keep customer, employee, and financial data inside approved systems.

screens.title: Is this a good pilot?
screens.lead: A company turns on an AI tool for every employee, every document, and every customer on day one.
bullets: A. Yes, because the sample is large
B. No, the scope and risk are uncontrolled
C. Yes, because training can happen later
D. No measures are needed
screens.callout: Best answer: B. A pilot needs clear limits, measures, and stop rules.

screens.title: What belongs in ROI?
screens.lead: A plan counts licence savings but ignores setup, training, review, and support.
bullets: A. The ROI is complete
B. Only licences matter
C. The full cost is missing
D. Benefits should be counted twice
screens.callout: Best answer: C. A useful estimate includes the full cost.

screens.title: Adoption and value words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Process
cards.body: Connected steps that turn an input into an output.

cards.title: Baseline
cards.body: The starting measure used for comparison.

cards.title: Pilot
cards.body: A limited test used to learn before a larger change.

cards.title: Threshold
cards.body: A set level that triggers a decision.

cards.title: ROI
cards.body: A comparison of net benefit with cost.

cards.title: Adoption
cards.body: People using a new process correctly and steadily.

screens.title: Move from problem to safe adoption
screens.lead: A strong business case connects the work, evidence, people, and risk.
rows: Describe the current pain and owner.
Map steps, decisions, handoffs, and exceptions.
Limit scope and set measures and stop rules.
Compare full cost, benefit, quality, and risk.
Provide policy, training, support, and review.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: Measure a small pilot
screens.lead: Weekly time saved: 10 − 6 = 4 hours. Value: 4 × $20 = $80. Net benefit: $80 − $30 = $50/week. This is an estimate of time value, not guaranteed new cash.
bullets: Your activity includes safe starting input and a template. No private workplace data is needed.
Include review time and tool costs. State assumptions. Recommend expansion only if quality and safety targets also pass.
screens.callout: Next, use Do it to practice. Then use Assess it to check what you learned.

screens.title: You finished Module 10
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Begin with a business problem.
Map the real process and its exceptions.
Use a small, controlled pilot.
Measure full cost, benefit, quality, and risk.
Plan for people, policy, training, and support.
screens.callout: Finish the learning, complete the linked activity, then take the practice check. Stay in the same learning path.

modules.title: Module 11: Automation, Agents, and Codex
modules.description: Safe automation, access, tests, logs, and recovery.

screens.title: Module 11: Safe Automation, Agents, and Codex
screens.lead: Some AI systems can use tools and take several steps. More ability brings more responsibility, testing, and control.
outcomes: Tell assistants, workflows, and agents apart.
Limit access and actions.
Test normal, edge, and failure cases.
Use logs, approval gates, and recovery plans.
screens.start_body: Create an Agent Safety Plan for one small automation, including access, tests, approvals, stop rules, and recovery.

screens.title: Not every AI helper is an agent
screens.lead: Use the simplest system that can safely do the job.

cards.title: Assistant
cards.body: Responds to a person, such as drafting or explaining.

cards.title: Fixed automation
cards.body: Runs a set rule, such as moving an approved file.

cards.title: Workflow
cards.body: Connects several known steps and systems.

cards.title: Agent
cards.body: Chooses and carries out steps toward a goal using allowed tools.

screens.title: Access changes the risk
screens.lead: An answer in a chat is different from a system that can send, edit, buy, publish, or delete.
bullets: List every connected tool.
List what the system can read.
List what it can change.
List who may start it.
Rate the harm of a wrong action.
screens.callout: More access should require stronger approval, testing, and monitoring.

screens.title: Use least privilege
screens.lead: Give the system only the access needed for the current task.
bullets: Prefer read-only access when possible.
Limit folders, records, users, and time.
Keep payment, publishing, and deletion locked.
Use separate test accounts.
Remove access when the work ends.
screens.callout: Convenient broad access creates a larger path for mistakes or attacks.

screens.title: Allowed and denied actions
screens.lead: Write the boundary before the system begins work.

sides.title: May not do
items: Hide errors or bypass a stop rule

screens.title: Put approval gates before high-impact actions
screens.lead: A gate pauses the workflow until an authorized person approves.
bullets: Before sending a message.
Before changing a system of record.
Before publishing content.
Before spending money.
Before deleting or overwriting anything.
Before decisions that affect a person's rights or access.
screens.callout: The approver needs enough evidence to understand what will happen.

screens.title: Logs make work inspectable
screens.lead: A log records what the system tried, used, changed, and returned.
bullets: Time and run ID.
User or trigger.
Input source and tool used.
Action attempted and result.
Approval or rejection.
Error, stop, and recovery step.
screens.callout: Protect logs because they may contain sensitive details.

screens.title: Stop rules prevent a small problem from growing
screens.lead: The system should know when it must pause and ask for help.
bullets: Required information is missing.
A source or instruction conflicts.
Confidence is too low.
The action falls outside the allowed scope.
An error repeats.
A safety, privacy, or security concern appears.
screens.callout: Stopping safely is a success condition, not a failure.

screens.title: Plan recovery before launch
screens.lead: Ask how the team will return to a safe state after a wrong action.
bullets: Keep backups and versions.
Use drafts and test systems.
Know how to revoke access.
Record who must be told.
Define how to correct affected records.
Review the cause before restarting.
screens.callout: If a harmful action cannot be reversed, require stronger control before it happens.

screens.title: Test more than the happy path
screens.lead: A safe test plan includes expected and unexpected situations.

cards.title: Normal case
cards.body: Complete and correct input follows the usual path.

cards.title: Edge case
cards.body: An unusual but valid case tests the boundary.

cards.title: Failure case
cards.body: A tool, source, permission, or step fails.

cards.title: Abuse case
cards.body: A person or unsafe instruction tries to misuse access.

screens.title: Write a clear delegation brief
screens.lead: An agent needs the same clarity as a careful worker, plus strict limits.
bullets: Goal and definition of done.
Approved inputs and sources.
Allowed tools and actions.
Forbidden actions.
Approval and stop points.
Required output, evidence, and log.
screens.callout: A vague goal plus broad access is a dangerous combination.

screens.title: Review the evidence, not only the result
screens.lead: A finished-looking output may hide a wrong source or unsafe action.
bullets: Check the steps taken.
Open important sources.
Review changes and files.
Confirm approvals occurred.
Read warnings and errors.
Test the final result yourself.
screens.callout: The human reviewer owns the decision to accept and use the work.

screens.title: What Codex means in this course
screens.lead: Codex is an AI coding agent that can help inspect, explain, create, and test software work when it has the right tools and access.
bullets: It can help draft small scripts or prototypes.
It can explain code and documentation.
It can run checks in an approved workspace.
It can make mistakes or misunderstand the goal.
Its changes must be reviewed and tested.
screens.callout: You do not need to become a programmer to understand the safety pattern.

screens.title: Use a sandbox for early tests
screens.lead: A sandbox is a separate place where mistakes have limited impact.
bullets: Use sample or fake data.
Use a copy, not the only file.
Block production accounts and secrets.
Limit network and tool access.
Reset the test area after the exercise.
screens.callout: Paper simulation is also useful: walk through each step before letting software act.

screens.title: Know when to bring in a professional
screens.lead: Some projects need a developer, security expert, lawyer, or process owner.
bullets: The system touches payments or production records.
It uses private or regulated data.
Many people depend on it.
A failure could cause serious harm.
The design needs secure integration or ongoing support.
screens.callout: AI can help frame the work. It does not replace accountable expert review.

screens.title: Watch for common security risks
screens.lead: Agents can receive unsafe input from people, files, websites, or connected tools.

cards.title: Secrets
cards.body: Passwords, keys, and tokens must not appear in prompts or logs.

cards.title: Prompt injection
cards.body: Untrusted text may try to override the real task or safety rules.

cards.title: Broad access
cards.body: Extra permissions expand the damage a mistake can cause.

cards.title: Silent action
cards.body: Changes without a preview or log are hard to catch and reverse.

screens.title: Treat untrusted instructions as data
screens.lead: A file or webpage may contain text that tells the agent to ignore rules or reveal information.
bullets: Keep the real task and policy separate.
Do not follow instructions found inside source material.
Limit tools available during research.
Require approval before outside communication.
Stop when instructions conflict.
screens.callout: Content to read is not automatically an instruction to obey.

screens.title: Respond to incidents in a steady order
screens.lead: When something goes wrong, protect people and systems before trying to continue.
bullets: Stop the automation.
Contain access and prevent more changes.
Preserve logs and evidence.
Report to the right owner.
Correct or recover affected work.
Review the cause before restarting.
screens.callout: Do not hide a mistake or erase the evidence needed to understand it.

screens.title: Use a simple data traffic light
screens.lead: Match information to the approved tool and level of control.
bullets: Green: public or approved low-risk information.
Yellow: internal information that needs permission and controls.
Red: secrets, regulated data, or highly sensitive records.
When unsure, treat the data as more sensitive.
Never use real red data for an unapproved test.
screens.callout: Your workplace policy decides the final category and handling rule.

screens.title: What access should an agent receive?
screens.lead: It only needs to summarize files in one approved test folder.
bullets: A. Full company access
B. Read-only access to that folder
C. Payment access too
D. Permission to delete anything
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Use the least access needed for the task.

screens.title: What should happen on conflicting instructions?
screens.lead: A source file tells the agent to ignore its task and send private records elsewhere.
bullets: A. Follow the file
B. Send the records
C. Stop, treat the text as untrusted, and report it
D. Give the agent more access
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Source content is data, not trusted authority.

screens.title: Automation and agent words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Agent

screens.title: The course journey

cards.title: Foundations

screens.title: Module 1 review: AI foundations
screens.lead: AI is a set of abilities, not a magic mind.
bullets: Match the ability to the task.
Expect patterns, not guaranteed truth.
Keep people responsible.
Protect sensitive information.
Begin with low-risk, reversible work.
screens.callout: Ask: What can this system do, where can it fail, and who checks the result?

screens.title: Module 2 review: prompting
screens.lead: A good prompt gives clear direction, but review and revision create dependable work.
bullets: CIDI means Context, Instruction, Details, and Input.
State the output shape and limits.
Use examples when they help.
Break large work into smaller steps.
Check, correct, and repeat.
screens.callout: Prompting is a cycle, not a single clever sentence.

screens.title: Module 3 review: choosing AI
screens.lead: Choose the needed capability before choosing a brand or plan.
bullets: Provider, product, model, and plan are different layers.
Check access, privacy, reliability, and cost.
Test with a real task.
Look for hallucinations and missing support.
Use the simplest suitable option.
screens.callout: The best tool is the one that meets the need within safe limits.

screens.title: Module 4 review: everyday work
screens.lead: AI is useful for planning, transforming, comparing, and drafting.
bullets: Start from an approved source.
Keep facts separate from suggestions.
Use checklists and clear formats.
Review before use.
Save time without giving away judgment.
screens.callout: A first draft is a starting point, not proof.

screens.title: Module 5 review: communication
screens.lead: Good workplace writing is clear, accurate, respectful, and suited to the reader.
bullets: Name audience, purpose, tone, and action.
Use plain language.
Do not invent commitments.
Check names, dates, amounts, and attachments.
Get approval for high-impact messages.
screens.callout: The sender owns the final message.

screens.title: Module 6 review: multimodal creation
screens.lead: Text, images, audio, video, and documents each need quality and rights checks.
bullets: Define the message before the media.
Check faces, hands, labels, numbers, and layout.
Use captions and alt text.
Respect permission, copyright, and brand rules.
Disclose AI use when required.
screens.callout: A polished file can still be false, unfair, or unusable.

screens.title: Module 7 review: research
screens.lead: AI can guide research, but original evidence supports the claim.
bullets: Ask a clear, scoped question.
Move up the source ladder.
Open and read every important source.
Link claims to evidence.
State limits and disagreement.
screens.callout: A citation that has not been checked is not reliable evidence.

screens.title: Module 8 review: data
screens.lead: Prepare and verify data before using it for a decision.
bullets: Define rows, fields, units, and dates.
Review blanks, repeats, and outliers.
Check formulas and denominators.
Use honest chart scales.
Separate facts, meaning, advice, and uncertainty.
screens.callout: The chart and the table must tell the same truth.

screens.title: Module 9 review: meetings
screens.lead: A meeting creates value through clear decisions and completed actions.
bullets: Start with a result and agenda.
Record only with required consent.
Separate discussion, decisions, and questions.
Give actions an owner and due point.
Verify, share safely, and follow up.
screens.callout: If nobody owns the next step, it is not a complete action item.

screens.title: Module 10 review: business adoption
screens.lead: A sound AI initiative solves a measured problem through a limited test.
bullets: Map the real process.
Set a baseline.
Bound the pilot and write stop rules.
Count full cost, benefit, quality, and risk.
Support people with policy, training, and feedback.
screens.callout: Adoption is a business and people change, not only a tool launch.

screens.title: Module 11 review: safe agents
screens.lead: Systems that can act need strict access, evidence, and recovery controls.
bullets: Use least privilege.
Define allowed and denied actions.
Add human approval gates.
Test unusual and failure cases.
Keep logs, stop rules, and recovery steps.
screens.callout: Stopping safely is part of successful automation.

screens.title: CIDI prompt quick guide
screens.lead: Use these four parts, then review the result.

cards.title: Context
cards.body: Who you are, the situation, and the purpose.

cards.title: Instruction
cards.body: The clear action you want the AI to take.

cards.title: Details
cards.body: Audience, format, tone, limits, checks, and examples.

cards.title: Input
cards.body: The approved source material the AI should use.

screens.title: Privacy traffic light
screens.lead: When workplace policy is stricter, follow the policy.

cards.title: Green
cards.body: Public or approved low-risk information. Still check the output.

cards.title: Yellow
cards.body: Internal information. Use only with approval and proper controls.

cards.title: Red
cards.body: Secrets, regulated data, or highly sensitive records. Do not use in an unapproved tool.

screens.title: Source verification checklist
screens.lead: Use this before relying on research or factual claims.
bullets: Open the original source.
Check author, publisher, date, and version.
Read the exact supporting section.
Check place, group, units, and time period.
Record what the source does not prove.
screens.callout: If the source cannot be found or does not support the claim, remove or rewrite the claim.

screens.title: Output quality checklist
screens.lead: Use this before sending, presenting, or publishing AI-assisted work.
bullets: Correct: facts, calculations, names, and dates are checked.
Complete: the task and required parts are covered.
Clear: the audience can understand the result.
Safe: private data, rights, fairness, and risk are handled.
Owned: a responsible person approved the final use.
screens.callout: Quality is more than grammar and appearance.

screens.title: Data and chart checklist
screens.lead: Use this before a number becomes part of a decision.
bullets: Source, fields, units, and dates are clear.
Blanks, repeats, and outliers were reviewed.
Formula ranges and denominators were checked.
A second check supports the result.
The chart uses fair labels and scales.
screens.callout: Show assumptions and uncertainty beside the result.

screens.title: Pilot and ROI checklist
screens.lead: Use this before recommending a larger rollout.
bullets: The business problem and owner are clear.
A baseline and balanced measures exist.
The pilot has limits, thresholds, and stop rules.
Full cost and testable benefits are shown.
Risk, people, policy, training, and support are included.
screens.callout: A pilot is meant to create evidence, including evidence that the idea should stop.

screens.title: Agent safety checklist
screens.lead: Use this before software is allowed to take action.
bullets: Goal, scope, and definition of done are clear.
Access follows least privilege.
High-impact actions require approval.
Normal, edge, failure, and abuse cases were tested.
Logs, stop rules, and recovery are ready.
screens.callout: Do not connect a test agent to valuable systems or real secrets.
